title: Pizza history: AI agent’s cardless purchase is a first for UK
summary: Papa John’s order was made without sharing bank security details – tech that could revolutionise shopping Retailers enter the unknown with AI shopping assistants on Black Friday An order of Papa John’s margherita pizzas has become the first purchase in the UK to be made using an AI agent using cardless payment technology. The order of nine mini pizzas was made as part of the Financial Conduct Authority’s (FCA) regulated sandbox trials to test the technology, using Lloyds Bank and payment specialist TrueLayer. title: ‘If the bot gets it wrong, who’s liable?’ Retailers enter the unknown with AI shopping assistants on Black Friday
summary: Brands know use of agents such as Meta Muse is on the rise but are unlikely to hand them the keys to the shop Have you downloaded Meta’s AI assistant Muse or do you plan to? They promise to find the best Black Friday deals, source Christmas gifts and find the ingredients for a romantic dinner. This week’s UK launch of the Muse AI assistant by the owner of Facebook and Instagram promises to transform how we shop – and how retailers make money. Continue reading...

title: Natural England objected to a datacentre. Weeks later ministers threatened to abolish the agency
summary: Body urged Bristol city council to reject plan because of risk to nearby protected wildlife and habitats Natural England objected to the building of a large AI datacentre near Bristol weeks before the government threatened to abolish the independent environmental adviser. The nature adviser made a significant intervention to urge Bristol city council not to grant planning permission for a 40MW datacentre at Avonmouth, because of the threat to protected wildlife and habitats at one of the UK’s most important sites for migratory birds, which is within 600 metres of the site. title: GTA in Istanbul? Meet the game developers bringing virtual crime chaos to their home cities
summary: From Helsinki to Istanbul, independent developers are putting Grand Theft Auto-style action on their home streets, and without billion-dollar budgets. They tell us how they do it Like most kids who shouldn’t have been playing Grand Theft Auto III in 2001, Eamonn Swayah imagined a version of Rockstar Games’ groundbreaking criminal sandbox set in his own back yard. In his case, that was a Manchester council estate, complete with local accents, driving on the left, and plenty of ways to hustle. He didn’t know it, but swapping the game’s facsimile of early 2000s New York City for a different setting was an idea he shared with many watchful game developers. Rockstar’s 3D open world template, it turned out, could be plonked in just about any location, so long as it had people and enough cars to run them over with. After GTA III attracted immense commercial success (and controversy), dozens of copycats and spiritual sequels hit the market throughout the 00s and 2010s. Gamers had a pithy name for them: “GTA clones”. Continue reading...
